20 — Volatility

Standard Deviation#

Heuristic1 min read
◆ The PatternHow widely values spread around their mean, the single number most of risk measurement is built on

// How widely values spread around their mean, the single number most of risk measurement is built on

Standard Deviation — the statistical building block of volatility measurement.

σ = √(Σ(x − μ)² / N)
where μ = mean, N = number of observations

Higher σ = more volatility = prices are spread far from the mean.

In markets:
• Historical Volatility = σ of returns × √252 (annualized)
• For normal data, 1σ covers ~68% and 2σ ~95% → the basis of Bollinger Bands
• 3σ events are "rare" but happen more often in markets than normal distributions predict (fat tails)
Worked example

Day 15: the last five closes (104, 102, 99, 101, 104) average 102.0. The deviations are 2, 0, −3, −1 and 2; squared, 4, 0, 9, 1 and 4; their mean is 3.6, and its square root 1.90. Measured on daily returns instead of prices it is about 2.6% a day — returns are what risk models use.

Where it misleads
  • It treats moves up and down alike, so a sharp rally counts as “risk” the same as a fall.
  • It assumes the spread is stable. Volatility clusters, so after a calm spell yesterday’s figure understates tomorrow’s.
  • Returns have fat tails: extreme days come far more often than a bell curve with this standard deviation predicts.
In code
df['sd5'] = df['close'].rolling(5).std(ddof=0)
df['ret_sd5'] = df['close'].pct_change().rolling(5).std()   # the same idea on returns

Sources
  • B. Mandelbrot, “The Variation of Certain Speculative Prices”, Journal of Business 36(4), 1963 — fat tails in prices
  • J. C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, Pearson — estimating volatility from returns
